chapters.title: Chapter 6: Risk Parity and Volatility-Weighted Allocation

lessons.title: Building a Simple Risk Parity Portfolio Across Nifty, Gold, and G-Secs

body.text: The inverse-volatility approximation from Lesson 1 is a reasonable starting point. Solving the actual risk parity condition, using the real covariance matrix rather than volatility alone, tells you something the approximation cannot: whether an asset's correlation with the rest of the book makes it a better diversifier than its volatility alone suggests, or a worse one.

children.text: This lesson solves true, correlation-aware risk parity across three of this course's core instruments, Nifty 50, Gold, and G-Sec futures, using Chapter 3's actual covariance matrix, and compares the result directly against the inverse-vol approximation from Lesson 1.
Setting Up the Problem: Reusing Chapter 3's Covariance Matrix

This is the same matrix from Chapter 3, restricted to these three assets. Nifty and G-Secs carry a modest negative correlation, Gold and G-Secs a modest positive one, exactly the relationships that will make true risk parity diverge from the simple inverse-vol approximation.

There is no simple closed-form solution once correlations are non-zero across more than two assets, so this is solved numerically: search for the weights that minimize the spread between each asset's risk contribution and the equal-risk target, subject to weights summing to 1.

body.code:
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

cov = np.array([
    [400,  19.2, -6],
    [19.2, 144,   18],
    [-6,    18,   36],
])  # Nifty, Gold, G-Sec, in %^2 units

def risk_contributions(w, cov):
    portfolio_var = w @ cov @ w
    marginal = cov @ w
    return w * marginal / portfolio_var  # each asset's share of total variance

def objective(w, cov):
    rc = risk_contributions(w, cov)
    target = 1.0 / len(w)
    return np.sum((rc - target) ** 2)  # minimize spread around equal risk

constraints = {"type": "eq", "fun": lambda w: np.sum(w) - 1}
bounds = [(0, 1)] * 3
w0 = np.array([1/3, 1/3, 1/3])

result = minimize(objective, w0, args=(cov,), bounds=bounds, constraints=constraints)
risk_parity_weights = result.x
body.caption: A standard risk parity solve: minimize the squared deviation of each asset's risk contribution from an equal 1/N target, subject to weights summing to 1 and staying non-negative.

children.text: The Result: True Risk Parity vs Naive Inverse-Vol

body.caption: Inverse-Vol Approximation vs Solved Risk Parity Weights

body.text: The solved risk parity weights are illustrative output representative of running the code above, not a hand-derived closed-form result. A real solver run on real data will converge to slightly different exact figures depending on the optimizer and data used; the direction and logic of the shift away from inverse-vol weighting is the point being demonstrated.

Nifty's weight rises under true risk parity, not because it became less risky, but because its modest negative correlation with G-Secs (-0.05) makes it a genuine diversifier the inverse-vol approximation could not see, since that approximation only looks at each asset's own volatility in isolation. Gold's weight falls slightly for the opposite reason: its positive correlation with G-Secs (0.25) makes it somewhat redundant with an asset already carrying a large weight in the book, so true risk parity trims it back relative to the naive approximation.

children.text: Verifying the Solution: Equal Risk Contribution Check

Any risk parity solve should be checked, not trusted blindly: compute each asset's actual risk contribution under the solved weights and confirm they land close to equal. Using weights of 18.5% Nifty, 26.0% Gold, and 55.5% G-Sec futures against this lesson's covariance matrix, the resulting risk contributions come out to roughly 14.0, 13.3, and 13.1 (in %² units), close to, though not perfectly, equal, consistent with a solver that has nearly, but not fully exhaustively, converged.

body.title: The Desk That Asked Why Nifty Got More Weight
body.scenario: A desk previously used inverse-vol weighting (16.7% Nifty, 27.8% Gold, 55.6% G-Sec) and switches to a properly solved risk parity portfolio, which assigns Nifty a higher weight, roughly 18.5%, and Gold a lower one, roughly 26.0%. A team member is confused: Nifty is still by far the most volatile of the three assets, so why would a risk-focused methodology give it more weight, not less?
body.prompt: Explain, using this lesson's covariance matrix, why true risk parity increases Nifty's weight relative to the naive inverse-vol approximation, despite Nifty remaining the most volatile asset in the book.
body.modelAnswer: Inverse-vol weighting looks only at each asset's own volatility and ignores how it relates to the rest of the portfolio. True risk parity accounts for the full covariance matrix, and Nifty carries a modest negative correlation with G-Secs (-0.05), meaning it tends to move slightly against the dominant G-Sec position rather than reinforcing it. That negative correlation genuinely reduces the marginal risk Nifty contributes to the combined book, relative to what its standalone volatility alone would suggest, so a correctly solved risk parity allocation rewards it with a somewhat larger weight to fully exploit that diversification value. Gold, by contrast, has a positive correlation with G-Secs (0.25), meaning it partially duplicates risk the book already carries through its large G-Sec position, so true risk parity trims Gold's weight slightly below what inverse-vol alone would assign it.

body.title: Computing Gold's Risk Contribution
body.prompt: Using the solved risk parity weights (Nifty 18.5%, Gold 26.0%, G-Sec 55.5%) and this lesson's covariance matrix, Gold's row-dot-weight value, (Σw)_Gold, works out to 50.98. What is Gold's risk contribution, RC_Gold = w_Gold × (Σw)_Gold? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 0.260 × 50.98 ≈ 13.25, which rounds to approximately 13.3. This sits close to Nifty's and G-Sec's own risk contributions (roughly 14.0 and 13.1 respectively), confirming the solved weights come close to satisfying the equal-risk-contribution target this lesson set out to achieve.

body.title: What True Risk Parity Sees That Inverse-Vol Cannot
body.question: Based on this lesson, what is the core piece of information true, correlation-aware risk parity uses that the inverse-vol approximation ignores?
options: The asset's trading volume on its home exchange
How each asset's covariance with every other asset in the portfolio affects its actual marginal contribution to total portfolio risk, not just its own standalone volatility
Whether the asset is denominated in INR or a foreign currency
body.explanation: Inverse-vol weighting uses only each asset's own volatility, treating every asset as though it existed in isolation. True risk parity uses the full covariance matrix, so an asset's actual marginal risk contribution depends on its relationship with every other asset in the book, not just its own volatility, which is exactly why Nifty's and Gold's weights shifted in opposite directions from the naive approximation.

points: Solving true risk parity requires numerical optimization once correlations are non-zero across more than two assets; there is no simple closed-form shortcut
A standard implementation minimizes the squared deviation of each asset's risk contribution from an equal 1/N target, subject to weights summing to 1
On this course's 3-asset covariance matrix, true risk parity gives Nifty a higher weight than inverse-vol weighting, because its negative correlation with G-Secs makes it a genuine diversifier
Gold receives a lower weight under true risk parity than inverse-vol, because its positive correlation with G-Secs makes it partially redundant with an asset already dominant in the book
Any solved risk parity portfolio should be verified by computing actual risk contributions under the solved weights and confirming they land close to equal
The direction of the shift away from inverse-vol weighting, not the exact decimal values, is what a systematic desk should take away from a risk parity solve on real data
